name: The engine runs on its own
what: A background engine owns every computer. The app and the command line are only clients, so quitting or crashing the app never stops a computer.
why: The product depends on it. Old lesson: the app failed to start its own engine in two live runs.

name: Every call and event defined once
what: Each thing the engine can be asked, and each thing it reports, is written down once. The app, the command line and their docs are generated from it.
why: The old contract was clean. New: one model in Zig, Swift types generated from it.

name: The VM runtime, packaged
what: Silo ships the program that runs each computer as its own virtual machine, pinned and checked.
why: Hard-won: 24 patches and 16,600 lines on top of MicroSandbox. Get as many accepted upstream as possible first.

name: The Linux image computers start from
what: One Ubuntu image, downloaded once in the background and checked, so a new computer is ready when you ask.
why: Small and proven. Keep the pinned checksum and the background download.

name: Create, start, stop and delete a computer
what: Make a Linux computer of a chosen size, start it, stop it, delete it. Inside, work runs as a normal user, not root.
why: Key every record by a stable id, never by name: the old code paid for that in every rename.

name: Run a command in a computer
what: Run a command inside and get its output and exit code. A long one keeps running if you disconnect.
why: Proven and clean in the old engine.

name: One silo command
what: A single command drives everything the engine can do, with machine-readable output on every command.
why: Every piece is proven here before it gets a screen.

name: A terminal into a computer
what: `ssh name.silo`, or one click, opens a shell in a computer in the terminal you already use.
why: Proven. The name follows the computer's id, so a rename never breaks it.

name: The Mac app: your computers
what: One window lists your computers with their state. Each has a page with Start, Stop and Terminal.
why: New, in Swift. The old web UI is 80,000 lines; start with the list and one page.

name: Long work you can follow
what: Anything slow shows progress, can be cancelled, waits its turn instead of failing as busy, and keeps its result across an engine restart.
why: Proven design. It is what makes the app feel reliable.

name: Recovery after a crash
what: If the engine dies in the middle of an operation, the next start finishes it or rolls it back.
why: In the new design this is a property the simulator checks, not code added afterwards.

name: A computer cannot reach your device
what: A computer reaches the public internet only: not your Mac, your local network, your VPN or cloud metadata.
why: A core guarantee, cheap when it is there from the first day.

name: Dev and production never mix
what: A development build has its own names, data and engine, so testing never touches the app you use.
why: Proven and small. Needed at once: the old Silo stays installed beside the new one.

name: Properties checked on every change
what: Each concept states what must always hold. A simulator runs random sequences of calls, crashes included, and checks it.
why: New. Takes over from most of the old live-check and CI machinery for logic errors.

name: Save and restore a checkpoint
what: Save a computer's state under a name and go back to it. A restore first saves where you were.
why: Proven. A restore must always save a recovery point first.

name: Fork a computer
what: Copy a computer, or one of its checkpoints, into a new independent computer for a task, and throw it away when done.
why: The heart of the product. Proven: 21 s from inside main.

name: Forks do not act twice
what: A fork gets a new identity, and its scheduled jobs and named services are off, so it never repeats what its source does.
why: Proven. Without it a fork sends the same emails and runs the same jobs as main.

name: See what was forked from what
what: A tree of your computers: which came from which, their state, and what is waiting.
why: Small and clean.

name: See everything a fork changed
what: The code, packages, settings, files and databases a fork changed since it was made, grouped so you can read it.
why: The part no other tool has. The approach is right; the code needs cleaning.

name: Merge a fork into main
what: Bring a fork's changes into the computer it came from. When main has not changed, everything applies and main keeps running.
why: The best code in the old engine: pinned to the diff you reviewed, undone cleanly if it crashes midway.

name: Undo a merge
what: Put a computer back to exactly how it was before its last merge.
why: Proven: 19 s. Small.

name: Credentials never come back in a merge
what: Logins, keys and credential files are never merged, and a merge that would carry them is refused.
why: A small guard with a large effect.

name: Install and open your agent
what: Pick Claude Code or Codex. Silo installs a checked version in the computer, and one action opens it there.
why: Proven: 14 s.

name: Silo's tools inside a computer
what: An agent inside a computer has the same silo command and MCP tools, reaching the engine through a channel only that computer can use.
why: Proven, and worth carrying over nearly as it is.

name: An agent never widens its own access
what: From inside, an agent may do anything that gives it no more than it has, and only on computers it made. Anything wider asks you.
why: The rule is sound; the old code is 6,400 lines of special cases. One rule, stated as a property.

name: Approvals only you can answer
what: A request that widens access waits. Silo shows what is asked in its own words, and you allow or deny with a note.
why: The agent is root in its computer, so the question must come from Silo, never from the agent's program.

name: Silo tells you when something waits
what: A notification and a menu bar item show what needs your answer and what finished or failed.
why: Approvals do not work if you have to watch the app.

name: Agents cannot fill your device
what: There is no cap on how many computers an agent makes. It is refused only when memory or disk would run out.
why: Decided on 10 Nov. Small.

name: First run makes main
what: Installing Silo, or one command, gives you main: created, started and reachable.
why: Proven from the command line: 58 s. The app's own first run was never driven.

name: GitHub access per repository
what: Sign in once, then choose per computer which repositories it may read or change. The computer never sees a real token.
why: Hard-won and good. Carry the design over.

name: Secrets an agent can use but not read
what: The computer sees a placeholder. The real value is swapped in only on its way to the hosts you allowed.
why: A core guarantee. The old docs record hard lessons on intercepting secure connections and echoed placeholders.

name: Forks get only the access you name
what: A fork starts with no secrets and read-only GitHub unless its parent hands over more, and never more than the parent has.
why: A property of the agent rule. Clean in the old code.

name: See what a computer holds
what: One view of a computer's secrets by name, its GitHub access, open ports and network rules.
why: Small, and it makes the access model visible.

name: Open a folder in your editor
what: One action opens a computer's folder in VS Code or Zed on your Mac.
why: The old code has 3,400 lines of editor profiles behind one command. Keep the command, cut the machinery.

name: T3 Code connects in
what: T3 Code stays on your Mac and works with the agent and the files inside main.
why: New. You named it as what stops you using Silo today.

name: Recipes: build once, fork fast
what: A short text file describes a computer. Silo builds it once, and every new computer made from it starts in seconds.
why: Small, clean and proven: 12 s per new computer.

name: One recipe for your whole setup
what: A recipe that gives a ready main: your agent, editor access, atelier, your repositories. Making one is guided, not a file written by hand.
why: New. You asked for it on 16 Nov.

name: Open a computer's website on your Mac
what: Publish a port from a computer. Each gets its own local address and is never exposed to your network.
why: Proven. Per-computer addresses let many forks serve the same port.

name: Network rules per computer
what: Each computer is open, limited to a list of hosts, or closed. An agent can ask for an addition.
why: Proven and clean.

name: Browse and copy files
what: See a computer's folders in the app and move files in and out.
why: Browsing is small. The old single-file copy is 3,600 lines over a second path; use one path.

name: Errors you can read
what: A failed action says why in one line, with details to copy, and stays next to what failed.
why: Cheap when every call returns a typed error from the start.

name: Merge when main has also changed
what: Changes come in item by item. Where both sides changed the same thing, you choose.
why: Built, never proven by a live run. This is where the simulator matters most.

name: A fork asks to merge, with a note
what: An agent or a job marks a fork as ready. You see it with a fresh diff and merge or decline.
why: Proven. It may fold into approvals: both are something that waits for you.

name: Replace main with a fork
what: Take a fork wholesale as the new main. The old main is kept aside.
why: 3,000 lines in the old code only because stores were keyed by name. With stable ids this is small.

name: Merge leaves the recipe alone
what: Merging a task changes main only. The saved recipe changes when you say so.
why: You decided this on 16 Nov. The old code added to the recipe on every merge.

name: Step history
what: Every command run through Silo is a numbered step, and you can fork from any step.
why: Clean and small. Not needed for the starter.

name: Many forks at once
what: Make several forks of one checkpoint in parallel, each running a command.
why: Small on top of fork.

name: Checkpoints that keep running programs
what: A checkpoint of a running computer keeps its memory, so a restore resumes where it was.
why: Built, not proven by a live run on Linux.

name: Old checkpoints give their disk back
what: Automatic checkpoints are kept to a number, and removing them really frees space.
why: Partial in the old code: the space did not always come back.

name: See which credentials a fork used
what: The diff shows which secrets a fork used, against which hosts and how often.
why: Useful when you review work done unattended.

name: Steps a recipe runs after a merge
what: A recipe can name what to run when a merge lands: migrate a database, restart a service.
why: Decide once real projects merge databases.

name: Open a pull request from a fork
what: Put a fork's code on a branch and open a pull request, with what was run attached.
why: The old one pushed from the device. With write access inside, the agent can do it itself.

name: Hide background noise in a diff
what: Measure what changes in an idle computer and leave that out of the diff.
why: Each measurement costs a whole extra fork and up to ten minutes. Filter known paths instead.

name: Fork and run a command
what: One command forks, runs something in the fork and returns its exit code.
why: Proven: 13 s from a checkpoint. The seed of every task.

name: Start a task with one call
what: One call names the recipe or checkpoint, what to run and where the result goes. The computer is removed when the task ends unless you keep it.
why: New. The pieces exist and nothing joins them. Removing the computer at the end is my recommendation, asked on the dashboard.

name: A record of each task
what: Each task keeps its status, timings, output, what it changed and which credentials it used.
why: New. The result has to live somewhere both the caller and you can read.

name: Tasks from GitHub events and schedules
what: A pull request, an issue label, a schedule or Fjord starts a task.
why: Your Fjord case. Keep triggers outside the engine: they only call 'start a task'.

name: Checks the agent cannot fake
what: The engine runs the tests in a fresh fork of the result, after the agent has stopped.
why: The lesson from dropping 'keep a fork when its tests pass': tests run inside the fork can be faked.

name: A ready computer per repository
what: A checkpoint with a repository installed and its tests passing, refreshed on a schedule, that tasks start from.
why: It is a recipe plus a schedule. Decide after the first real tasks.

name: Task time limits and a queue
what: A task stops at a time limit, and tasks wait their turn for memory and disk.
why: Needed once tasks run with nobody watching.

name: GitHub Actions jobs in fresh computers
what: Each job of a private repository runs in a fresh computer made from a recipe.
why: 7,500 lines of clean Go that passed 19 of 19 live. It becomes one trigger on top of tasks.

name: Task templates and follow-ups
what: Named instructions for recurring work, and a review comment that becomes a follow-up task.
why: Ideas only. They need task records first.

name: Host computers on a Linux server
what: A Linux server runs the engine as a service and hosts computers with nobody logged in.
why: Proven. One Zig engine built for both systems makes this cheaper than before.

name: Connect another device
what: Link another Mac or Linux machine so this Silo manages its computers.
why: 11,000 lines in the old code and no recorded run across two real devices. Design it again, small.

name: Computers on other devices, same as local
what: Every command and the app's list work on a computer wherever it runs.
why: It falls out of the design when the app is only a client of an engine.

name: Answer approvals from another device
what: Requests waiting on a server can be answered from your Mac.
why: Needed for a server with no screen.

name: SSH into a computer from another machine
what: Turn on SSH for a computer on your network, with a key you hand out.
why: Built, never proven, and it overlaps with connecting a device.

name: A dedicated agent machine, or several
what: A Mac mini or a server set up to run tasks, and tasks spread over several machines.
why: Ideas. Mostly setup and docs on top of the entries above.

name: Signed releases
what: A versioned, signed and notarized app and engine, built the same way every time.
why: Hard-won tooling. 81 changes were never released from the old tree.

name: Updates
what: Silo checks for a signed update and installs it when you say.
why: Needed before anyone else uses it.

name: Give disk space back
what: See what each computer takes on your disk and release what is unused.
why: Proven. Disk is the first thing that fills up.

name: Keep a computer current
what: Silo's own parts inside a computer update at start. The system is rebuilt on the newest image while keeping your work.
why: Proven for Linux. It matters once main has lived for weeks.

name: Logs you can search
what: Search and save the output of a computer and of Silo itself.
why: Built. Start with the engine's own log from the command line.

name: Updates keep computers running
what: An engine update pauses each computer, swaps the engine and resumes them.
why: 6,300 lines, never run across two real versions. Start with stop, update, start.

name: Change a computer's size
what: Change the CPUs, memory and disk of a stopped computer.
why: Built, small.

name: Computers that start with your device
what: Chosen computers start when the engine starts.
why: Built, small.

name: Settings
what: Theme, startup, which terminal and editor to use, how much memory and disk to keep free.
why: Add each setting with the entry that needs it, not as a page built up front.

name: Who did what
what: Every call that changed something, or was refused or held, with who made it: you, another device, or a computer.
why: Nearly free if the engine keeps one ordered log of everything that happened.

name: Isolation tests anyone can rerun
what: A script plays a hostile agent inside a computer and tries every boundary.
why: It exists and was run. It backs each 'cannot' with evidence.

name: What comes out of a computer is not trusted
what: Output, file names, screens and web pages from a computer are bounded and shown as plain data.
why: A rule for every client from the first day, not a feature added later.

name: What Silo does not protect, stated plainly
what: The threat model says what an agent can still do: send out data it can read, misuse access it was given.
why: Already written. Honest docs were a strength of the old project.

name: A private channel for Silo's tools
what: Each computer reaches the engine through a private socket, not a port open on your device.
why: Planned. It needs a patch to the VM runtime.

name: Agent logins that do not travel
what: A Claude or Codex sign-in does not end up in forks and exports by accident.
why: Open since 10 Nov. Removing login files afterwards was shown not to work.

name: Stop every agent at once
what: One action stops every computer and blocks every secret and token.
why: An idea. Small once the engine owns all state.

name: Only known programs drive the engine
what: Programs on your device are identified before the engine listens to them.
why: Needs signed releases first.

name: Fewer, plainer approval requests
what: Similar asks from one task become one decision, in plain words.
why: An idea. Decide after living with approvals.

name: Limits set once for the whole device
what: One file outside every computer sets ceilings: network mode, allowed hosts, repositories.
why: An idea, for a team.

name: See what a computer looked up
what: Each computer's name lookups are logged, with names off its list flagged.
why: Planned.

name: An independent security review
what: A specialist firm reviews the parts that hold the guarantees.
why: For when a company asks. Not code.

name: Measurement, reports and release paperwork
what: Reports on agent work, opt-in usage counters, a bill of materials per release, governance files.
why: They serve selling a pilot, not the product. Revisit when a customer asks.

name: A desktop in a Linux computer
what: A computer can run a graphical desktop that you and its agent share.
why: Built and heavy. Take it when GUI automation inside main comes next.

name: See and use a computer's desktop
what: A window on your Mac shows the computer's screen, with sound and resize.
why: 9,000 lines, and the proven runs used a viewer that was later replaced.

name: Agents drive the desktop
what: An agent inside a computer can look at its screen, click and type, asking you first unless you allow it.
why: Only ever tested against a fake engine.

name: Copy, paste and drop files into the desktop
what: Move text, images and files between your Mac and a computer's desktop.
why: Comes with the viewer.

name: macOS computers
what: Make a macOS computer on an Apple Silicon Mac, set up with no clicks, and start, stop and delete it.
why: 44,000 lines of Rust driving Apple's framework through bindings. A small Swift helper per computer replaces that.

name: Checkpoint and fork a macOS computer
what: Save a macOS computer with its memory in seconds, and fork it.
why: Checkpoints are proven. The fork flow was redone and not checked again.

name: Terminal, files, network and secrets for macOS
what: A macOS computer gets the same terminal, editor, files, ports, GitHub access, secrets and network rules as a Linux one.
why: The rule is one kind of computer. Its network gateway alone is 6,500 lines.

name: A macOS computer's screen
what: A native window shows the macOS computer's display, with copy and paste.
why: Proven and small. Natural in a Swift app.

name: Developer tools in macOS computers
what: A macOS computer comes with Command Line Tools, Git, Node and your agent.
why: Built.

name: macOS on another Mac, bigger disks, shared folders
what: View a macOS computer that runs on another Mac, grow its disk, share a folder into it, export it.
why: Never run on two real Macs. The rest are ideas.

name: Share a computer as a file
what: Export a whole computer to one file and import it elsewhere as a new computer.
why: 22,000 lines across three formats, plus 4,400 to recover an interrupted export. One format, no recovery machinery.

name: Search and jump to anything
what: One shortcut finds every page and every action.
why: Proven and small. Natural once there are many actions.

name: Menus, shortcuts and help
what: Native menus, keyboard shortcuts and a bundled guide.
why: Add them with the screens they belong to.

name: GitHub with a personal token
what: Use your own GitHub token for a computer. It is stored as an ordinary secret.
why: Decided on 10 Nov: a token is a secret bound to GitHub's hosts. Nothing special to build.

name: Container computers
what: On a Linux host, a lighter and less isolated kind of computer.
why: You kept it as a choice on 10 Nov. It is about 19,000 lines for a second runtime, so it comes last.

name: Exact rebuilds of a recipe
what: A recipe rebuilt later or elsewhere gives identical tools, for example with Nix.
why: An idea.

name: Back up and restore a whole host
what: Save the engine's state and base computers and restore them on a new machine.
why: An idea.

name: Website and public docs
what: A landing page with a read-only demo, and a README that says what Silo is today.
why: Both are out of date. Rewrite once the starter exists.

name: Exports without your logins
what: An export leaves your sign-ins out.
why: A check showed the removed logins are still in the file. Solve it through logins that do not travel.

name: Push to GitHub through your device
what: A commit leaves a computer through your Mac, with your Mac's credentials.
why: About 5,000 lines for what write access inside the computer already does.

name: Moving old saved data
what: Screens and code that convert data from earlier versions of Silo.
why: Nothing to migrate when starting from an empty tree.

name: The Silo app on Linux
what: A Linux build of the desktop app, with packages and an updater.
why: Dropped on 4 Nov. Linux gets the engine and the command line.

name: A hosted AI reviewer
what: A hosted service that reads a fork's diff and returns findings.
why: Set aside on 10 Nov. Never deployed.

name: A project folder on your Mac
what: A .silo folder in a repository, and forking a local folder.
why: Dropped on 10 Nov: it assumes the code and the agent live on your Mac.

name: OpenClaw and Hermes recipes
what: Built-in recipes for two resident chat agents.
why: Set aside on 10 Nov.

name: Requests through a shared folder
what: The first way a computer reached the engine: request files in a shared folder.
why: Replaced by the per-computer channel.

name: Other ways to run computers
what: E2B as the VM backend, forks that carry memory, one image cache shared by several engines.
why: Studied and rejected, or left out on purpose.

name: Earlier desktop and computer-use stacks
what: KasmVNC, Luda, the ChatGPT app and a native display stream.
why: Each was replaced.

name: Small leftovers
what: The backup page, the alpha banner, the glass window effect, copying production settings into Dev, an earlier GitHub Action, bandwidth limits.
why: Removed, cosmetic, or tied to the old layout.
